title: Why say yes to a fussy buyer?
principle: Tough buyers make you better. Seek them out.

screens.text: Let me tell you about Indian bike riders in the 1980s. They watched every rupee spent on petrol. About 9 in 10 two-wheelers had two-stroke engines, which used more petrol. In 1985, Hero Honda launched the CD 100, India's first four-stroke bike. It went about 80 km a litre.

screens.prompt: These riders cared a lot about petrol costs. What do you think their demands helped Hero Honda become?

options.label: Famous for the lowest bike prices
A big seller of bikes outside India
The biggest bike maker in India

screens.why: Riders wanted to go as far as possible on one litre of petrol, so Hero Honda had to make bikes that used less petrol. That helped it sell more bikes. By 2009, it sold about half of India's motorcycles, and it had been the world's biggest two-wheeler maker for eight years.

screens.title: Demanding buyers
screens.text: That wasn't luck. In 1990, Michael Porter, a Harvard professor, studied why some countries make better products. One answer was demanding buyers at home: buyers who want more push companies to improve faster than easy buyers do. So don't run from tough buyers. Learn from them.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: Your home bakery can learn from tough buyers too. It's December, your fifth year. A nearby hotel wants 15 cakes a week at ₹700 each. Its rules: hair nets, the fridge temperature written down daily, a date on every cake and monthly kitchen checks. Your kitchen needs ₹30,000 of work.

screens.prompt: The hotel buys 15 cakes a week at ₹700. Each costs ₹400 to make. The kitchen fix is ₹30,000. How many weeks to earn it back?
screens.why: Exactly. You earn ₹300 on each cake, so 15 cakes give you ₹4,500 a week. ₹30,000 ÷ ₹4,500 is about 7 weeks. After that, the fix has paid for itself, and your kitchen is better for other orders too.

wrong.a: I see what you did: ₹30,000 ÷ ₹10,500, the hotel's whole weekly payment. But ₹400 of each ₹700 pays for the cake. You keep ₹300 × 15 = ₹4,500 a week, so about 7 weeks.
wrong.c: That's ₹30,000 ÷ ₹400, one cake's cost. But you keep ₹300 on each of 15 cakes, so ₹4,500 a week. ₹30,000 ÷ ₹4,500 is about 7 weeks.

screens.prompt: Not every tough buyer helps you. I'll show you six buyers. For each one, tell me: will they make you better, or only cost you?

items.text: A hotel that checks your kitchen every month
A buyer who wants ₹200 off every time
A café that sends back cakes that don't match
A shop that pays you 90 days late
A mother who needs every ingredient listed, for her child's allergy
A buyer who wants free delivery across town

screens.why: Exactly. Some buyers ask for better quality: a clean kitchen, cakes that match and clear ingredient lists. Meeting them makes every cake better. Other buyers only ask for lower prices or more time to pay, and that just leaves you with less money.

screens.prompt: For the hotel, you now put a date on every cake and write down fridge temperatures. How does this affect your other orders?

options.label: Your other orders take more time
Your other cakes become better too

screens.why: Right. You use the same kitchen for every order. Dates on cakes help you use older cream first, and daily temperature checks warn you if the fridge gets too warm, before cream goes bad. One tough buyer's rules improved all your orders.

wrong.a: You don't run two kitchens. Once every cake has a date and the fridge is logged, all your cakes are made the better way, and less goes bad.
wrong.b: Writing a date takes a few seconds a cake. And with dates on everything, you use the oldest cream first, so less goes bad. All your cakes get better.

screens.prompt: Your friends say your cakes are perfect, but the hotel's chef finds three problems. Whose words will help you improve more?

options.label: The chef, who has tried many bakers' cakes
Your friends, who already buy your cakes

screens.why: Right. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Kind words cost nothing and teach you nothing. The chef's three problems are three things to fix before other buyers find them.

wrong.a: Your friends are kind. But remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. The chef's three problems tell you what to fix.
wrong.c: What sells matters. But the chef's three problems are what will keep cakes selling. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. A tough buyer's notes tell you what to fix.

screens.setup: It's mid-December. The hotel wants cakes before Christmas. To meet its rules, you must spend ₹30,000 on a second fridge and steel tables. The work takes a week, so it can be ready just in time, but only if you start now.
screens.question: What do you tell the hotel?

options.label: Accept, and fix the kitchen in January
options.outcome: You deliver the Christmas cakes and earn ₹9,000 in two weeks. But at the first kitchen check, the inspector finds one fridge that's too full and wooden tables. The hotel stops ordering from you.
options.why: You took the order but not the standard. A tough buyer only makes you better if you meet its rules.
options.better: Say yes, fix the kitchen this week, then start.

options.label: Refuse, because the rules are too strict
options.outcome: You keep your ₹30,000 and your old ways. Nothing goes wrong. But the hotel buys from a bigger bakery, and your kitchen stays as it was.
options.why: Saying no was safe, but you turned away the buyer most likely to make you better.
options.better: Say yes, fix the kitchen this week, then start.

options.label: Accept, but start once the kitchen is fixed
options.outcome: You fix the kitchen in a week and start just before Christmas. You earn ₹4,500 a week, so the ₹30,000 comes back in about 7 weeks. You pass every check, and less cream goes bad across all your orders.
options.why: Exactly. You met the tough standard before you started, so the hotel stayed, and every customer got a better cake.

screens.text: A café returns any cake that leans. It is tough on ___. A buyer who wants ₹200 off every order is tough on ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Porter called the first kind demanding buyers. Meeting them makes you better. The second kind only makes you poorer.

summary: Demanding buyers (Michael Porter): buyers who want more push you to get better.
Seek buyers who are tough on quality. Avoid buyers who are only tough on your price.
Meet the tough standard before you start, and every customer gains.

cards.front: A hotel wants your cakes but checks your kitchen monthly. What should you do?
options: Meet its standard, then say yes
cards.back: Tough buyers make you better. Seek them out.

cards.front: Which tough buyer helps you most?
options: One who wants ₹100 off every time
One who sends back anything uneven
cards.back: Buyers tough on quality make you better. Buyers tough on price just cost you.

cards.front: Kitchen fix ₹20,000. A new buyer leaves you ₹4,000 a week. Weeks to earn it back?

sources.label: Michael Porter, The Competitive Advantage of Nations (Harvard Business Review, March 1990)
